title: Traditional Rajasthani Butterfly Wing Mehndi Design for Back Hand
descriptionParagraphs: A beautiful rajasthani mehndi design tailored for the back of the hand, featuring petal arrangement and wave pattern. Rated as Expert, this pattern is perfect for Karva Chauth.

Skin on the back of the hand is thinner than the palm, so the stain is usually lighter and fades sooner. Leaving the paste on for longer helps the colour develop. This is a detailed pattern usually done by an experienced artist; allow plenty of time and work in small sections.
Rajasthani, or Marwari, mehndi is known for dense, very fine detail that covers the whole hand. Sojat, in Rajasthan's Pali district, is India's best-known henna-growing area.
Application tips: Divide the hand into panels first and fill one at a time. Allow plenty of time, since dense coverage takes much longer than open styles.

image.alt: Rajasthani Butterfly Wing mehndi design for back hand — traditional henna pattern

faq.q: Why does my mehndi look orange at first?
faq.a: Fresh henna stains are orange. The colour deepens to reddish brown over the next 24 to 48 hours as the dye oxidises.

faq.q: Is black henna safe?
faq.a: Natural henna is never black. Products sold as black henna often contain PPD, a hair-dye chemical that can cause skin reactions, so they are best avoided.

faq.q: How can I make my mehndi darker?
faq.a: Leave the paste on longer, seal it with lemon and sugar, keep the skin warm, and avoid water for the first day after removing the paste.

title: Delicate Rajasthani Butterfly Wing Mehndi Design for Full Hand
descriptionParagraphs: A mesmerizing rajasthani mehndi design providing full hand coverage, featuring mesh jaal and dotwork. Rated as Medium, this pattern is perfect for an engagement.

Full-hand designs run from the fingertips to the wrist, so allow extra time for application. Work from the wrist towards the fingers, or the other way round, so you never rest on wet paste. This pattern suits someone who is already comfortable with basic lines, dots and petals and wants to practise even spacing.
Designs often include figures such as a bride and groom, peacocks and elephants. Mirrored designs, where the two hands form one picture when held together, are a hallmark of the style.

Application tips: Leave the paste on for at least four to six hours; the longer it stays, the deeper the stain. Dab a lemon and sugar mixture on the dried paste to keep it moist and stuck to the skin.

image.alt: Rajasthani Butterfly Wing mehndi design for full hand — delicate henna pattern

faq.q: Is black henna safe?
faq.a: Natural henna is never black. Products sold as black henna often contain PPD, a hair-dye chemical that can cause skin reactions, so they are best avoided.

faq.q: How can I make my mehndi darker?
faq.a: Leave the paste on longer, seal it with lemon and sugar, keep the skin warm, and avoid water for the first day after removing the paste.

faq.q: Should I do a patch test before applying mehndi?
faq.a: Yes. Apply a small amount of the paste to the inner arm and wait 24 hours, especially if you have sensitive skin or are using a new cone.

The soles take henna as well as the palms do, while the top of the foot stains lighter. Stay seated and avoid walking until the paste has dried completely. This is a beginner-friendly pattern: practise the main shapes on paper first, then copy them onto skin with a fine-tipped cone.
